title: The hammer and the feather
body: In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the Moon. With no air to slow the feather, both hit the ground at the same moment, just as Galileo predicted. From 1.5 m the fall takes about 1.36 s on the Moon and 0.55 s on Earth.

source.label: NASA NSSDC: The Apollo 15 Hammer-Feather Drop

pipNote: Arm wanted to race a feather, but up here it is always a tie.

photo.caption: Apollo 15, 1971: David Scott drops a hammer and a feather on the Moon.

title: Endless shadows at the south pole
body: Near the lunar south pole the Sun never climbs more than about 2 degrees above the horizon (2.05° in 2028 at this spot), and it circles the sky once a month. A 1 m rock can cast a shadow tens of metres long. The sun position in this game comes from real NASA/JPL Horizons data for this exact spot.

source.label: NASA GSFC PGDA: Lunar Polar Illumination

pipNote: Here even a pebble gets a shadow long enough to brag about.

photo.caption: The Moon's south pole seen by NASA's Clementine, a mosaic of about 1,500 images.

title: Anorthosite: the Moon's ancient crust
body: The bright lunar highlands are made of anorthosite, a rock that floated to the top of a global magma ocean more than 4 billion years ago. Apollo 15 brought back a famous piece, sample 15415, nicknamed the Genesis Rock.

source.label: NASA Lunar Sample Compendium: 15415

pipNote: Genesis Rock sounds like a rock band, and Arm already wants to join.

photo.caption: Apollo 15 sample 15415, the 'Genesis Rock', made of anorthosite.

title: Why the Moon is silent
body: Sound is a vibration that travels through air, water or solid things. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so outside your helmet there is total silence. You only hear sounds through your radio, or vibrations travelling through your own suit when you touch something.

source.label: NASA Science: Moon Facts

pipNote: Out here I could sing very badly and only your radio would know.

photo.caption: Apollo 17, 1972: Harrison Schmitt beside the flag, in total silence.

title: The dust that fought Apollo 17
body: Lunar dust is sharp like broken glass because there is no wind or water to round it off, and it clings because it carries electric charge. On Apollo 17 a broken rover fender sprayed dust everywhere, so the crew built a new fender from maps and tape. Dust also made gear overheat by covering radiators.

source.label: NASA Science: Lunar Dust and Duct Tape

pipNote: Fixing a rover with maps and tape is my kind of engineering.

photo.caption: Apollo 17, 1972: Gene Cernan inside the lunar module after a dusty moonwalk.

title: Tracks that last for ages
body: With no wind and no rain, footprints and wheel tracks on the Moon are only slowly erased by tiny meteorite impacts. The bootprints left by Apollo astronauts more than 50 years ago are still there today and may last for millions of years.

source.label: NASA Science: Apollo 11 Bootprint

pipNote: Better make your bootprints neat, because the Moon keeps them for ages.

photo.caption: Apollo 11, 1969: a bootprint pressed into lunar soil.

title: The Electrodynamic Dust Shield
body: NASA's Electrodynamic Dust Shield uses electric fields to push dust off surfaces like glass and radiators. In March 2025 it worked on the Moon for the first time, aboard Firefly's Blue Ghost lander. Keeping solar panels clean could decide whether a lunar robot lives or dies.

source.label: NASA: Dust shield successfully repels lunar regolith

pipNote: An electric broom with no bristles has Arm worried about its job.

photo.caption: An Electrodynamic Dust Shield in a NASA Kennedy lab, 2023.

title: Talking to Earth takes time
body: The Moon is about 384,400 km away. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so a message takes about 1.28 s to reach Earth and the same to come back: about 2.6 s between your question and Houston's answer. From the south pole, Earth also sinks below the horizon for days at a time.

source.label: NASA/JPL Horizons System

pipNote: That pause is not Houston thinking; the message is still flying home.

photo.caption: Deep Space Network antenna DSS-53 in Madrid, which talks to spacecraft far away.

title: Hot on one side, frozen on the other
body: Without air to spread heat around, a surface facing the Sun can reach about 115 C while its shadowed side drops far below -100 C. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter measured craters near the poles colder than -240 C, among the coldest places in the solar system.

source.label: NASA Science: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter

pipNote: Half of me wants a fan and the other half wants a blanket.

title: Who is MICA?
body: MICA and Pip are made up for this game. But the problem MICA faced is real: lunar robots lose power when dust covers their solar panels or when long shadows fall, and several real landers never woke up again. Solving that is one of the open challenges of NASA's Artemis program.

source.label: NASA Artemis

pipNote: Okay, confession: MICA and I are made up, but the dusty-panel problem is real.

title: Stuck in soft ground
body: In April 2009, NASA's Spirit rover broke through a crust at a site on Mars called Troy and dug its wheels into soft sand. It never got out. Stuck, it could not tilt its solar panels toward the winter Sun, and it fell silent on March 22, 2010. Soft, steep regolith is still one of the biggest dangers for any rover.

source.label: NASA JPL: NASA's Spirit Rover Completes Mission on Mars

pipNote: Spirit, I wish I could have lent you my winch.

photo.caption: NASA illustration: computer model of Spirit's wheels sunk in soft Martian soil, 2009.

title: Tracks that are not tracks
body: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter camera has photographed boulders, some 7 to 9 meters wide, that rolled down crater walls and left smooth, curving trails, "like a marble rolled down a pile of sand." With no wind or rain to erase them, such trails last for a very long time, and from a distance they can look a lot like vehicle tracks.

source.label: LROC (LRO Camera team): Rolling Rolling Rolling

pipNote: Note to self: not every track has a driver, some just have gravity.

photo.caption: Boulder trails on a lunar slope, seen by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

title: What happened to the 1969 flag?
body: The flags are too small for NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to see, but not their shadows: photographing the Apollo sites at different times of day, scientists watched small shadows circle the flagpoles. The flags of Apollo 12, 16 and 17 are still standing. Apollo 11's flag was knocked over by engine exhaust when the crew lifted off, as Buzz Aldrin reported. After decades of harsh ultraviolet light and extreme temperatures, the nylon is probably badly faded.

source.label: NASA SSERVI: Apollo Moon Flags Still Standing

pipNote: Spying on flags by watching their shadows is the sneakiest science ever.

photo.caption: Apollo 11, 1969: Buzz Aldrin beside the flag at Tranquility Base.

title: When Earth sets
body: Seen from the lunar south pole, Earth is above the horizon only about half of each month, and even then it hangs low, where a hill can hide it. That is why NASA is planning relay satellites over the south pole (the Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems project), so Artemis crews can talk to Earth even when it is out of view.

source.label: NASA: Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS)

pipNote: When Earth hides behind a hill, I chat with Arm until it returns.

photo.caption: A crescent Earth above the lunar horizon, photographed by Apollo 17 in 1972.

title: Ice in the dark
body: On October 9, 2009, NASA's LCROSS mission crashed a spent rocket stage into Cabeus, a permanently shadowed crater near the lunar south pole, and flew through the plume of debris. Analysis found roughly 6% water in the impact area, including nearly pure ice crystals in some spots. Ice in these cold traps is a big reason Artemis is going to the south pole.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Water Ice on the Moon?

pipNote: Who knew crashing a rocket on purpose could be such good science?

title: Why VIPER's solar panels stand up
body: NASA's VIPER rover carries its solar panels on its sides, not on top, because at the lunar south pole the Sun never climbs high: 10 or 11 degrees at most where VIPER was meant to drive, and only about 2 degrees here, almost on the pole. A flat panel facing up catches just a few percent of that grazing light (sin 2° ≈ 3.5%), while a panel standing upright and facing the Sun catches nearly all of it. MICA, a fictional older rover in this game, had flat panels. Pip learned from that.

source.label: NASA podcast: Houston We Have a Podcast, VIPER

pipNote: MICA's flat panels taught me to stand up straight and face the Sun.

photo.caption: A VIPER test rover with its upright solar panels at NASA Glenn, 2022.

title: Radiation on the lunar surface
body: In 2019 the Chinese lander Chang'e 4 carried a German-built detector (LND) to the Moon's far side. It measured an average dose of about 1,369 microsieverts per day on the surface, and the daily cosmic-ray dose there is around 2.6 times the dose inside the International Space Station. Solar storms add sudden bursts on top of that.

source.label: Zhang et al. 2020, Science Advances: First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface

pipNote: Invisible stuff zooming through us all day is why I love my shelter.

title: A blanket of Moon soil
body: During a solar particle storm, protons reach the Moon from almost every direction, so the shadow of a boulder does not protect you. A thick cover of lunar soil (regolith) over a shelter does. Since the 1980s NASA studies have modelled how much regolith a lunar base needs to keep its crew safe during solar proton events.

source.label: NASA NTRS: Solar-flare shielding with regolith at a lunar-base site (1988)

pipNote: I piled this soil blanket myself, and it is my proudest pile of dirt.

title: A sundial that never stops turning
body: At the lunar south pole the Sun glides all the way around the horizon about once a month, never more than a few degrees up. Long shadows rotate across the ground like the hand of a clock, about 12 degrees a day. That is how MICA's photos could be put back in order.

source.label: NASA SVS: Lunar South Pole Illumination with Earth and Sun

pipNote: Forget wristwatches: at this pole every rock becomes a clock hand.

title: Peaks of light, pits of darkness
body: Because the Moon's axis is tilted only about 1.5 degrees, some spots near the poles sit in permanent shadow while nearby ridges stay sunlit for most of the year. Scientists stacked about 1,700 orbital images over six months to map how often every spot is lit. Whether the Sun reaches you depends on the hills around you, which is why this camp goes dark for days even though the Sun has not set for the whole region.

source.label: LROC: South Pole Illumination Map

pipNote: Hills here play hide-and-seek with the Sun, even when it has not set.

photo.caption: The lunar south pole from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, 2010.

title: Sleeping through the lunar night
body: Away from the poles a lunar night lasts about 14 Earth days and gets bitterly cold. Small landers without nuclear heaters are not expected to survive it, yet Japan's SLIM lander woke up again after three lunar nights in 2024, surprising its own designers. At the south pole, hills can bring a 'night' of just a few days, like the one at our camp.

source.label: SpacePolicyOnline: SLIM Does It Again — Survives Another Lunar Night (2024)

pipNote: Knowing SLIM woke up makes my own nap through the dark less scary.

title: Earthshine
body: Sunlight bouncing off Earth lights up the Moon's night side with a faint ashen glow. Leonardo da Vinci explained it more than 500 years ago. How bright it is depends on Earth's phase seen from the Moon: during our camp night Earth sat close to the Sun in the sky, so it was only a thin crescent and its light was very weak.

source.label: NASA APOD: The Da Vinci Glow (2025)

pipNote: Earthshine is home leaving a tiny night-light on for us.

photo.caption: A crescent Moon and Venus from the Space Station, 2003; the dark part glows with earthshine.

title: Real story: Pragyan, 2023
body: In August 2023 India's Chandrayaan-3 put the Vikram lander and the little Pragyan rover down near the lunar south pole. Pragyan's laser instrument made the first measurements on the surface there and confirmed sulphur in the soil, something orbiters could not do.

source.label: ISRO: LIBS confirms the presence of Sulphur on the lunar surface

pipNote: Little rover, big laser, sulphur found: small robots for the win!

title: Real story: SLIM, 2024
body: Japan's SLIM, the 'Moon Sniper', landed on 20 January 2024 and proved a pinpoint landing: JAXA estimated its accuracy at about 10 m or better, maybe 3–4 m, against a 100 m goal. It later survived several lunar nights.

source.label: JAXA press release, 25 January 2024

pipNote: Moon Sniper is a great nickname; Arm suggests calling me Pip the Precise.

title: Real story: Odysseus, 2024
body: On 22 February 2024 Intuitive Machines' Odysseus became the first commercial spacecraft to soft-land on the Moon, near the crater Malapert A in the south pole region. A leg broke and it tipped over, but it still sent back NASA science data.

source.label: NASA: First surface science in decades via commercial Moon mission

pipNote: Tipped over and still did its job, Odysseus is my kind of hero.

title: Real story: the dust shield works, 2025
body: In March 2025 NASA's Electrodynamic Dust Shield flew on Firefly's Blue Ghost lander. Using electric fields, it lifted lunar dust off glass and a thermal radiator on the real Moon, just like you cleaned MICA's panels.

source.label: NASA: Dust shield successfully repels lunar regolith on the Moon

pipNote: Turns out you cleaned MICA just like a real Moon experiment, high five!

photo.caption: Jan 2025: the rocket carrying Blue Ghost and NASA's dust shield waits to launch.

title: Real story: Artemis IV
body: NASA is targeting early 2028 for Artemis IV, the first Artemis landing: two astronauts will descend to the surface and spend about a week near the lunar south pole. In this game you stayed much longer, through 11 weeks and a long night. That part is fiction, for now. The game also sets the mission in September to December 2028 for the best sunlight at the pole, while NASA's real target is early 2028.

source.label: NASA: Artemis IV

pipNote: Our long stay is pretend for now, but I am saving you a bunk.

photo.caption: April 2026: the Artemis II crew photographs Earth setting behind the Moon.

title: Tranquility Base
body: On 20 July 1969 the Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility, at 0.67° N, 23.47° E. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked there while Michael Collins circled overhead in the command module. The dark 'seas' you see from orbit are old lava plains, smoother than the bright highlands.

source.label: NASA NSSDC: Apollo 11 lunar landing mission

pipNote: No water in these seas, just old lava, so no swimming, Arm.

photo.caption: Apollo 11, 20 July 1969: Buzz Aldrin works beside the lunar module Eagle.

title: Program alarm 1202
body: During Apollo 11's descent the guidance computer flashed alarm 1202: it was overloaded with too much data and could not process it all. After a few seconds of analysis, Mission Control's Charlie Duke told the crew they were GO. The computer kept running its most important jobs and dropped the rest. Later Armstrong flew the last part by hand to avoid a boulder field.

source.label: NASA: 50 Years Ago, One Small Step, One Giant Leap

pipNote: My circuits flash a 1202 too when everyone asks me questions at once.

title: The rocket equation
body: A rocket pushes by throwing propellant out of its nozzle, so it gets lighter every second it burns, and the same push speeds it up more and more. NASA writes the ideal rocket equation as Δv = vₑ · ln(m_full / m_empty). In this game the lander has a game-sized 120-tonne dry mass and an exhaust speed of 3.7 km/s: rounded numbers, not real Starship figures.

source.label: NASA Glenn: Ideal Rocket Equation

pipNote: Throwing stuff backward to go forward still feels like magic, but it is math.

photo.caption: 16 July 1969: the Saturn V lifts Apollo 11 off toward the Moon.

title: Apollo 12 and Surveyor 3
body: In November 1969 Apollo 12 set down about 155 m from the robot lander Surveyor 3, which had been sitting on the Moon since 1967. Pictures from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter still show the ground around Apollo 12 brightened by the rocket exhaust blasting the surface. With no air to slow it, plume dust flies fast and far, so future Moon bases will need landing pads well away from camp.

source.label: NASA: LRO looks at Apollo 12 and Surveyor 3 landing sites

pipNote: Rule for future bases: land far away, or you sandblast your neighbors.

photo.caption: Apollo 12, 1969: Alan Bean at Surveyor 3, with the lunar module behind.

title: Twilight rays: still a mystery
body: About 10 seconds before lunar sunrise or sunset, Apollo 8, 10, 15 and 17 crews saw pale streamers rise over the horizon, and the Apollo 17 astronauts sketched them. One idea is that sunlight charges the ground so tiny dust grains float up and scatter light. The Moon's thin gases are not enough to explain it. NASA's LADEE orbiter was sent in 2013 to test the dust idea, and scientists still argue about the answer.

source.label: NASA Science: Mission to study mysterious lunar twilight rays

pipNote: Maybe floating dust, maybe not, and even the scientists are still arguing.

photo.caption: NASA's Clementine, 1994: light glowing above the Moon's dark edge.

title: Apollo's Moon buggy
body: Apollo 15, 16 and 17 each carried a Lunar Roving Vehicle. It weighed 210 kg, had a 2.3 m wheelbase and two side-by-side seats, and ran on two non-rechargeable 36-volt batteries. Its 82 cm wheels were woven from zinc-coated steel wire, with titanium chevrons for grip. Crews drove 27.8 km on Apollo 15, 26.7 km on Apollo 16 and 35.9 km on Apollo 17.

source.label: NASA NSSDC: Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle

pipNote: Woven wire wheels, like a picnic basket that can drive, I want one!

photo.caption: Apollo 15, 1971: James Irwin with the Lunar Roving Vehicle.

title: A rover for Artemis
body: In April 2024 NASA picked three companies (Intuitive Machines, Lunar Outpost and Venturi Astrolab) to develop a Lunar Terrain Vehicle that can handle the extreme conditions at the south pole. NASA plans crewed drives from Artemis V, and between missions the rover can drive itself to do science. The rover in this game is imagined: its look, its 18 km/h top speed and its 20° slope limit are game choices.

source.label: NASA: NASA Selects Companies to Advance Moon Mobility for Artemis Missions

pipNote: A rover that drives itself between missions might finally be my racing buddy.

photo.caption: 2026: NASA astronauts test a lunar terrain vehicle prototype.
